los.text: Describe the causes (eg. Helicobacter pylori, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, smoking), signs and symptoms, and diagnosis of peptic ulcer disease (PUD) and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD)
los.html:
PUD causesH. pylori (~90% DU, ~70% GU), NSAIDs/aspirin, smoking, alcohol, steroids + NSAID, SSRIs + NSAID, Zollinger–Ellison (gastrinoma), stress (ICU, burns: Curling's).
Symptoms
  • Epigastric pain
  • Duodenal typically better with food and worse at night
  • Gastric worse with food.
  • Bloating, nausea.
  • Complications: haematemesis/melaena, perforation (sudden severe pain, peritonism), gastric outlet obstruction (vomiting).
GORDHeartburn, acid regurgitation, worse lying flat/after meals; atypical: chronic cough, hoarseness, nocturnal asthma, dental erosion.
Risk factors (GORD)Obesity, hiatus hernia, pregnancy, smoking, alcohol, fatty meals, drugs relaxing the LOS (CCBs, nitrates, anticholinergics).
Diagnosis
  • H. pylori urea breath test or stool antigen (stop PPI 2 weeks, antibiotics 4 weeks before).
  • OGD if red flags (ALARMS: Anaemia, Loss of weight, Anorexia, Recent onset/progressive, Melaena/haematemesis, Swallowing difficulty) or age ≥55 with weight loss.
  • GORD is often a clinical diagnosis
  • pH/impedance monitoring if unclear.
NICE 2-week-wait OGD: dysphagia at any age, or ≥55 with weight loss + upper abdominal pain/reflux/dyspepsia.

los.text: Explain the pathophysiology of PUD and GORD
los.html:
Ulcers form when aggressive factors outweigh mucosal defence.
DefencesMucus–bicarbonate layer, tight junctions, epithelial renewal, mucosal blood flow, prostaglandins (PGE2/PGI2) which ↑ mucus/HCO₃⁻ and blood flow and ↓ acid.
  • H. pylori: urease makes NH₃ (neutralises local acid), flagella, adhesins
  • CagA/VacA toxins → inflammation.
  • Antral gastritis → ↓ somatostatin → ↑ gastrin → ↑ acid → duodenal ulcer.
  • Pangastritis → atrophy → gastric ulcer, adenocarcinoma, MALT lymphoma.
NSAIDsCOX-1 inhibition → ↓ protective prostaglandins + direct topical injury.
GORD
  • Transient LOS relaxations, ↓ LOS tone, hiatus hernia (loss of crural diaphragm), impaired oesophageal clearance, delayed gastric emptying
  • → acid/pepsin/bile damage squamous mucosa
  • → oesophagitis
  • → stricture or Barrett's (intestinal metaplasia → adenocarcinoma risk).

los.text: Apply the pharmacology of drugs used to treat PUD and GORD and relevant evidence for their benefits to be able to choose and manage effective treatment for individual patients
los.html:
ClassExampleMechanismNotes
PPIOmeprazole, lansoprazoleIrreversibly block H⁺/K⁺-ATPase in parietal cells (prodrug activated by acid)Most effective. Long-term: C. difficile, hypomagnesaemia, ↓B12, fractures, hyponatraemia. Omeprazole ↓ clopidogrel activation (CYP2C19)
H2 antagonistFamotidineBlock parietal H2 receptors → ↓ histamine-driven acidLess potent; tachyphylaxis
Antacid/alginateGavisconNeutralise acid; alginate raft over stomach contentsQuick symptom relief
Prostaglandin analogueMisoprostolRestores PGE1 protectionDiarrhoea; abortifacient (avoid in pregnancy)
ProkineticMetoclopramideD2 antagonismExtrapyramidal effects; short courses only
H. pylori eradication (UK)
  • 7-day triple therapy = PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin or metronidazole (penicillin allergy: PPI + clarithromycin + metronidazole).
  • Retest with UBT if symptoms persist.
Bleeding ulcerResuscitate, Glasgow–Blatchford score, endoscopy within 24 h (endoscopic therapy), PPI after endoscopy if high-risk stigmata.
GORD
  • Lifestyle (weight loss, raise bed head, avoid late meals) → full-dose PPI 4–8 weeks (8 weeks if oesophagitis) → lowest effective dose.
  • Surgery: laparoscopic fundoplication.

los.text: Describe the basic mechanisms of swallowing, gastroesophageal reflux and vomiting
los.html:
Swallowing
  • (1) oral (voluntary): bolus pushed back by tongue.
  • (2) Pharyngeal (reflex, swallowing centre in medulla): soft palate seals nasopharynx
  • Larynx elevates
  • Epiglottis covers it
  • Vocal cords close
  • Breathing stops
  • UOS (cricopharyngeus) relaxes.
  • (3) Oesophageal: primary peristalsis (vagus, myenteric plexus)
  • LOS relaxes via NO/VIP (receptive relaxation).
Anti-reflux barrierLOS tone, crural diaphragm "pinchcock", acute angle of His, intra-abdominal oesophagus, phrenoesophageal ligament.
RefluxMostly during transient LOS relaxations; cleared by secondary peristalsis and swallowed salivary bicarbonate.
Vomiting
  • Coordinated by the vomiting centre (medulla, nucleus tractus solitarius).
  • Inputs: chemoreceptor trigger zone (area postrema, outside BBB: D2, 5-HT3, NK1; drugs and toxins)
  • Vagal afferents from the gut (5-HT3; chemotherapy, distension)
  • Vestibular system (H1, muscarinic; motion)
  • Higher centres (anxiety, smells).
SequenceSalivation, retching, deep breath, glottis closes, diaphragm and abdominal muscles contract against a relaxed LOS/stomach.

los.text: Describe the role of the stomach in the digestion and absorption of nutrients
los.html:
Storage (receptive relaxation via vagus) and mixing/grinding (antral peristalsis) to form chyme; pylorus meters small amounts into duodenum.
Secretions
  • HCl from parietal cells (kills microbes, denatures protein, activates pepsin, aids iron absorption Fe³⁺ → Fe²⁺)
  • Pepsinogen from chief cells → pepsin (protein digestion begins)
  • Intrinsic factor (B12 absorption in ileum)
  • Gastric lipase
  • Mucus/HCO₃⁻
  • Gastrin (G cells), somatostatin (D cells).
Acid regulation
  • Cephalic (vagal ACh, ~30%), gastric (distension, peptides → gastrin, ~60%), intestinal (inhibitory: secretin, CCK, GIP, somatostatin).
  • Parietal cells are stimulated by ACh (M3), gastrin (CCK2) and histamine (H2, from ECL cells).
AbsorptionMinimal. Only lipid-soluble substances such as alcohol and aspirin.
EmptyingSlowed by fat, acid and hyperosmolar chyme in the duodenum (enterogastric reflex, CCK, GIP).

los.text: Explain the role of the small intestine in the digestion of proteins, fats and carbohydrates
sessions: BMS 2: Digestion in the small GI
los.html:
Proteins
  • Pepsin starts it.
  • Pancreatic trypsinogen is activated by brush-border enteropeptidase (enterokinase) → trypsin, which activates chymotrypsin, elastase, carboxypeptidases.
  • Brush-border peptidases → amino acids (Na⁺-coupled transporters) and di/tripeptides (PepT1, H⁺-coupled), hydrolysed inside the cell.
Carbohydrates
  • Salivary + pancreatic α-amylase → maltose, maltotriose, α-limit dextrins.
  • Brush border: lactase, sucrase-isomaltase, maltase.
  • Glucose/galactose via SGLT1, fructose via GLUT5, out via GLUT2.
Fats
  • Bile salts emulsify
  • Pancreatic lipase + colipase
  • → monoglycerides + free fatty acids
  • → micelles
  • → diffuse into enterocyte
  • → re-esterified in SER
  • → chylomicrons (with apoB-48)
  • → lacteals
  • → thoracic duct.
  • Short/medium-chain FAs go straight to portal blood.
Hormonal controlCCK (fat/protein in duodenum → pancreatic enzymes + gallbladder contraction), secretin (acid → pancreatic HCO₃⁻).
Malabsorption causesPancreatic insufficiency (CF, chronic pancreatitis → steatorrhoea), bile salt deficiency (cholestasis, ileal resection), mucosal disease (coeliac), lactase deficiency.

los.text: Describe the pathology of diseases of the oesophagus (achalasia, varices, oesophagitis, tumours) and stomach (gastritis, ulcers, gastric tumours)
los.html:
Oesophagus

Achalasia
  • Loss of inhibitory neurons in myenteric plexus → LOS fails to relax + aperistalsis.
  • Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the start, regurgitation.
  • Barium "bird's beak"
  • Manometry diagnostic.
  • Rx: pneumatic dilatation, Heller myotomy, POEM, botox.
VaricesPortal hypertension → dilated submucosal veins at the porto-systemic anastomosis (left gastric → azygos). Massive haematemesis.
OesophagitisReflux (basal hyperplasia, elongated papillae, eosinophils), eosinophilic (atopic, >15 eos/hpf, food bolus), infective (Candida, HSV, CMV in immunosuppressed), pill-induced.
Barrett'sSquamous → columnar epithelium with goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia).
TumoursSquamous cell carcinoma (upper/middle third; smoking, alcohol, hot drinks, achalasia) vs adenocarcinoma (lower third; GORD, Barrett's, obesity; now commoner in UK).

Stomach

Gastritis
  • Acute (NSAIDs, alcohol, stress)
  • Chronic type A autoimmune (body/fundus, anti-parietal cell & anti-IF antibodies → pernicious anaemia, achlorhydria, ↑gastrin), type B bacterial (H. pylori, antrum), chemical/reactive (bile, NSAIDs).
Peptic ulcer
  • Punched-out defect through muscularis mucosae
  • Base of necrotic debris → granulation tissue → fibrosis.
  • Complications: bleeding (posterior DU erodes gastroduodenal artery), perforation, stricture.
  • Biopsy gastric ulcers to exclude cancer.
Tumours
  • Adenocarcinoma (intestinal type, linked to H. pylori/atrophy; diffuse type with signet ring cells → linitis plastica; Virchow's node)
  • MALT lymphoma (H. pylori; may regress with eradication)
  • GIST (c-KIT, interstitial cells of Cajal)
  • Neuroendocrine tumours.
